q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE push factor that drove migration to industrial cities in the period c. 1750 to c. 1900.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why industrial cities grew so rapidly despite terrible living conditions, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which governments responded to the problems of industrial cities in the period c. 1750 to c. 1900.

sample_answers.a: Enclosure of common lands and the spread of commercial agriculture displaced rural laborers who could no longer support themselves on the land, forcing them to seek wage work in towns.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, factories concentrated where coal, transport, and labor were available, and workers kept coming because even miserable urban wages were more reliable than the starvation facing them in the countryside — the city offered survival, not comfort.
sample_answers.c: Governments passed public health acts, built sewers and water systems, and regulated housing and factory conditions (such as Britain's Public Health Act of 1848 and later tenement laws) after epidemics and investigations exposed urban squalor.

q1.stimulus:
Historians explain the explosive growth of industrial cities as the result of powerful push and pull factors operating together. In the countryside, enclosure movements and commercial agriculture displaced millions of peasants who could no longer live off the land, while population growth meant that rural areas could not absorb all their children. At the same time, factories concentrated in towns near coalfields, ports, and railway junctions, offering the one thing the countryside increasingly could not: regular cash wages. Migrants therefore flooded into cities not because urban life was attractive — the slums, disease, and pollution were notorious — but because the alternative was worse. The result was the fastest urbanization in human history, with cities growing far beyond the capacity of their housing, sanitation, and government.
—Historian's account of urbanization in the period c. 1750–1900

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE feature of working-class housing in Manchester described by Engels.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which industrial urbanization affected workers' health.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Engels's account, though vivid, may not represent the experience of all city dwellers.

sample_answers.a: Engels describes cramped, poorly built cottages crowded into courts and alleys with no ventilation, no sewers, and piles of refuse — housing thrown up as cheaply as possible for maximum profit.
sample_answers.b: Overcrowded, unsanitary housing bred cholera, typhus, and tuberculosis; polluted water and air, combined with exhaustion from long factory hours, produced death rates in industrial districts far above those of the countryside.
sample_answers.c: Engels was a revolutionary seeking to expose capitalism's failures, so he emphasized the worst slums; skilled workers, clerks, and shopkeepers lived in better conditions, and his account generalizes from Manchester's poorest districts.

q2.stimulus:
The working-class districts of Manchester are built in the most unsystematic manner. Unpaved, unsewered courts are crowded with cottages whose walls are thin and whose cellars are damp. In these narrow alleys the air is stagnant and foul, for there is no ventilation and refuse of every kind accumulates. Whole families inhabit single rooms, and in the cellars beneath, where the damp rises through the floors, human beings live crowded together in conditions that would sicken any observer. The landlords, who never visit these properties, draw their rents with perfect indifference to the misery they produce.
—Adapted from Friedrich Engels, The Condition of the Working Class in England, 1845

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the photograph that illustrates overcrowding in industrial cities.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the tenement conditions shown in the photograph.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which photographs like Riis's influenced responses to urban poverty.

sample_answers.a: The narrow alley is packed with tenement buildings whose windows and fire escapes crowd every inch of space, with laundry lines strung across — showing how landlords subdivided buildings to house the maximum number of tenants.
sample_answers.b: Mass immigration (to New York) combined with low wages meant that poor families could only afford tiny rented rooms; landlords profited by packing as many tenants as possible into buildings never designed for such density.
sample_answers.c: Riis's flash photographs made middle-class viewers confront slum conditions they had never seen, generating public outrage that pressured politicians to pass tenement-house reforms and building codes.

q3.stimulus: The image is Jacob Riis's 1890 photograph Bandits' Roost, showing a crowded alley in New York City's Mulberry Street tenement district. Riis, a Danish-American journalist, used the new technology of flash photography to document the inside of tenements and slum alleys. His book How the Other Half Lives (1890) exposed the living conditions of immigrants and the urban poor to a shocked middle-class audience.
